trial.failure_analysis: Investigation failed or produced no valid diagnosis. | Workflow error: {"code": "ValueError", "message": "HYBRID_TOOL_BUDGET_EXCEEDED"}

stop_conditions: Two independent sources confirm whether the primary bottleneck is the product database query path or the Redis catalog cache miss path (e.g., metrics + database/Redis inspection), and the evidence agrees.
The apparent db_qps increase is explained as cache stampede after catalog_ttl expiry, or refuted by a stable database-side metric and stable Redis hit/miss ratio across repeated snapshots.
No new latency or error dependency is identified after three trace/edge paths are checked from gateway through order-service and inventory-service to postgres/redis.
A strong unresolved evidence conflict appears, such as healthy pool/error metrics alongside consistently degraded request latency, requiring a different evidence class before continuing.
initial_hypotheses: In inventory-service, product lookups are dominated by a database path: db_qps rises from ~0.15 to ~135 while Redis keyspace misses far exceed hits (~187k vs ~44k), so a rapidly expiring catalog TTL (30s) is causing cache misses that fall through to repeated single-product queries (320 calls/1s).

Postgres is a shared candidate bottleneck: the same product query is executed heavily and all five request-path services depend on it, but active_sessions is empty and HTTP error rates are 0.00%, so this may be latency pressure rather than failure.

Order-service checkout latency is propagated, not primary: the critical path shows gateway POST /checkout (55.8ms) routing through order-service (42.4ms) then inventory-service GET /products (22.5ms), consistent with inventory/database delay propagating upward.

notification-service may be under-instrumented rather than unhealthy: only 2 requests / ~0.07 rps observed and an empty Redpanda consumer lag, so its low throughput needs independent confirmation before any incident attribution.

arguments.hypothesis: inventory-service GET /products performs an N+1/loop of single-product SELECTs against Postgres because the catalog cache is not effective (misses ≫ hits), driving inventory-service db_qps from ~0.15 to ~243 (320 calls/s of "SELECT id,name,price,stock FROM products WHERE id=$1") and propagating ~22ms latency up through order-service checkout to gateway; no errors anywhere.
arguments.root_cause: inventory-service's GET /products product-lookup path falls through to Postgres with a per-product query loop rather than serving from cache. Two independent sources agree: (1) metrics show inventory-service db_qps exploding from a ~0.145 baseline to ~243 (relative change ~1670x, trend increasing) while every other service's db_qps is flat or slightly decreasing, and (2) the Postgres pg_stat_statements one-second delta attributes 320 calls of the single statement "SELECT id,name,price,stock FROM products WHERE id=$1" per second — by far the dominant DB work — with a tiny 0.046ms mean exec time, i.e. a high call count rather than a slow-query problem. The trace critical path confirms the direction of causality: gateway POST /checkout (55.8ms) → order-service POST /checkout (42.4ms) → order-service GET (23.7ms) → inventory-service GET /products (22.5ms), with only a 0.35ms SET cache write, so the dominant nested latency originates inside inventory-service's product read path; gateway and order-service are upstream propagation, not origin. All services report error_pct 0.00 and no error spans, so this is a load/latency amplification on the DB read path, not an outage. The immediate mechanism is a hot fan-out of single-key product reads reaching Postgres (N+1-style per-product lookup), which the cache is not absorbing; the exact precondition that made the cache ineffective (catalog TTL expiry/keyspace miss burst) is consistent but only partially corroborated by the evidence I hold.
llm_findings: Only inventory-service db_qps is anomalous (baseline 0.145 → current 243, increasing); gateway ~0.16 and all other services flat/down — DB read pressure is localized to inventory-service.

Postgres 1s delta: 320 calls of "SELECT id,name,price,stock FROM products WHERE id=$1" (mean 0.046ms) is the dominant work — a call-count explosion, not a slow query; pg_sleep calls_delta 0 rules out injected DB stalls.

Trace chain gateway POST /checkout 55.8ms → order-service 42.4ms → inventory GET /products 22.5ms with a 0.35ms cache SET confirms inventory-service is the origin of nested latency, gateway/order-service are propagation.
145 inventory requests vs 71 order requests in the same window indicates multiple product reads per checkout (fan-out), consistent with per-product single-key SELECTs.
All services error_pct 0.00 with zero error spans → latency amplification on the read path, not failure/pool exhaustion.
notification-service at 2 requests/~0.07 rps cannot be classified from this evidence; no incident attribution made.
arguments.recommended_fix: 1) Fix the access pattern: batch product lookups in inventory-service GET /products with a single "WHERE id = ANY($1)" query (or fix the cache to serve the whole product set), instead of one SELECT per product. Code patch to inventory-service is plausible but out of inspection scope here, so remediation is operational + a targeted code change to the product-read path. 2) Restore cache effectiveness: use cache-aside with a longer catalog TTL, negative caching, and per-key jitter/request coalescing (single-flight) so a TTL expiry cannot stampede Postgres. 3) Verify with: inventory-service db_qps returning toward ~0.15 baseline, pg_stat_statements calls_delta for the single-key SELECT dropping, and a stable/improved Redis hit:miss ratio over repeated snapshots rather than cumulative counters. 4) Confirm the single-row SELECT uses the products primary-key index so 320 calls/s stays cheap while the batching fix lands.
arguments.reasoning_summary: Metrics: only inventory-service db_qps is anomalous (0.145 → 243, increasing); gateway db_qps is ~0.16 and all other services are flat/slightly down, so the DB read pressure is localized to inventory-service. DB inspection: the 1s delta shows 320 calls of the single-row product SELECT (dominant work, 0.046ms mean) — a call-count explosion, not a slow query. Trace: the longest nested chain is gateway → order-service → inventory-service GET /products (22.5ms) with a 0.354ms cache SET, confirming inventory-service is the origin of nested latency and gateway/order-service are propagation. Mapping totals: 145 inventory requests vs 71 order requests in the same 20s window is consistent with order-service issuing multiple product reads per checkout (fan-out), matching the 320 calls/s of the single-key SELECT. HTTP errors 0.00% everywhere and empty error spans indicate latency amplification, not failure or pool exhaustion (no pg_sleep activity: calls_delta 0). No contradicting evidence found; the cache-ineffectiveness precondition is inferred, not directly measured.
remaining_uncertainty: Redis hit/miss counters cited in my hypothesis came from cumulative keyspace stats; I could not re-read the inspect_redis page within budget, so cache-miss dominance is only weakly corroborated and the 30s TTL value is unverified.

The inventory-service source for get_products could not be read (get_code_symbol/search returned no source in scope), so the per-product query loop is inferred from the 320 calls/s single-key SELECT plus the request-count fan-out rather than from code.
No fresh second metrics snapshot was taken, so the db_qps elevation is confirmed inside one 20s window plus a 1s DB delta; chronic vs transient cannot be distinguished.
notification-service shows only 2 requests / ~0.07 rps; whether it is under-instrumented or genuinely idle is unresolved.
